paragraphs: This paper studies how a neural network’s depth and width affect the functions it can represent. Its focus is depth separation: situations where reducing the number of layers requires a large increase in width. The authors investigate these trade-offs through dynamical systems, connecting neural network approximation to what happens when a continuous function is repeatedly applied to its own output.

The key mathematical objects are periodic points, which return to their starting value after repeated applications of the function. The authors derive width requirements that depend on the period and hold for L1 approximation error, strengthening earlier results based on classification error. They also sharpen width lower bounds enough to establish exponential depth-width separations in regimes where earlier results did not apply.

The analysis connects a function’s periods, its Lipschitz constant, and the growth of oscillations under repeated composition. A further result identifies a universal constant governing the trade-offs when the function has odd periods. These are theoretical statements about representational requirements: they clarify when extra depth can substantially reduce the width needed for approximation.
icml-2020-better-depth-width-trade-offs-.tldr: Dynamical-systems analysis strengthens theoretical bounds on how much wider certain neural networks must become when their depth is reduced.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether overfitting can be detected using only a trained model and its training data. The proposed approach, Counterfactual Simulation, follows training examples through the model, identifies rarely occurring patterns, and perturbs them. This examines the model’s internal handling of its examples rather than relying on performance on a separate test set or bounds derived from model complexity.

Applying the procedure to logic circuits gives a version with no hyperparameters that works across neural networks, random forests, and lookup tables. In experiments, these circuit representations alone distinguish models with different degrees of overfitting. The method does not need access to the original high-level architecture, making circuits a common representation for comparing otherwise different kinds of models.

Those comparisons also suggest that stochastic gradient descent finds shared patterns rather than simply performing brute-force memorization, even when neural networks are trained on randomized labels. In this respect, the observed networks resemble forests. The authors also identify a limitation that makes their proposal unsuitable in an adversarial setting, so its empirical diagnostic success does not establish robustness against deliberate manipulation.
icml-2020-circuit-based-intrinsic-method.tldr: Counterfactual Simulation detects differences in overfitting by perturbing rare patterns inside circuit representations of models using only training data.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to assign candidates to multiple positions when evidence arrives as pairwise contests. Each observation reveals which of two candidates wins at one position. Candidate-position possibilities form a bipartite graph, and the goal is to identify the best overall matching with high probability after collecting comparisons. The challenge combines uncertainty about preferences with the combinatorial structure of the assignment.

The authors consider two definitions of a winner: Borda and Condorcet. For the Borda case, they reduce the problem to an existing combinatorial bandit formulation. This yields both probably approximately correct and exact algorithms, with polynomial computation per round. Their sample requirements resemble those of the original formulation and are nearly optimal for a subclass of problems.

For the Condorcet case, the authors first develop a fully polynomial approximation scheme for the offline problem where winning probabilities are known. They then use it as an oracle inside CAR-Cond, an exploration algorithm with a sample-complexity analysis. The stated advance is the first algorithm for identifying the Condorcet winner in this setting with polynomial running time per round.
icml-2020-combinatorial-pure-exploration.tldr: The paper develops computationally efficient algorithms for identifying candidate-position matchings from noisy pairwise comparisons under Borda and Condorcet winner criteria.

paragraphs: Feature-attribution explanations assign importance scores to the inputs behind a prediction. This paper examines two desirable properties: sparsity, where few features receive substantial importance, and stability, where small input changes produce similar explanations. The authors connect these properties to adversarial training, which trains a model against bounded input perturbations.

For a class of one-layer networks that includes logistic regression, they establish two results using Integrated Gradients. Training against an adversary bounded in the infinity norm produces sparse attribution vectors. They also show that ordinary training with an added explanation-stability penalty is equivalent to adversarial training in the analyzed setting. This provides a theoretical link between a training procedure and the character of its explanations.

Experiments extend the sparsity finding to deep networks on standard image datasets and to DeepSHAP attributions. Adversarially trained models produce substantially sparser explanations with little loss on natural test data, and outperform ordinary L1-regularized training on attribution sparsity. The broader deep-network finding is empirical; the stated equivalence involving stability is proved for the specified one-layer class.
icml-2020-concise-explanations-of-neural.tldr: Adversarial training can produce sparser feature explanations, with theoretical results for one-layer networks and empirical support for deeper models.

paragraphs: This paper addresses bias that can arise when datasets overrepresent or underrepresent social groups. It proposes a preprocessing framework that learns a new data distribution with controlled group representation and target fairness properties, such as statistical parity. At the same time, the framework aims to remain close to the empirical distribution of the original dataset.

The approach expresses bias-mitigation goals as constraints on a maximum-entropy distribution. Among distributions satisfying those constraints, it selects one closest to a specified prior in KL divergence. This makes the desired adjustments explicit rather than treating preprocessing as an unspecified balancing operation. The main computational contribution is a construction for the authors’ chosen constraints and priors that runs in time polynomial in the data dimension.

In the reported experiments, samples from the learned distribution attain the desired representation and statistical rates. Classifiers trained on those samples retain fairness properties while showing only a slight accuracy loss. These results support the framework as a way to make targeted changes to training data while preserving much of its predictive usefulness.
icml-2020-data-preprocessing-to-mitigate.tldr: A maximum-entropy preprocessing framework adjusts group representation and fairness statistics while keeping the learned data distribution close to the original.

paragraphs: This paper replaces a single decision-making agent with a society of simple, specialized agents pursuing their own objectives. The central challenge is incentive alignment: local self-interest must support the overall sequential decision problem. Understanding that relationship is difficult because the equilibrium behavior of a non-cooperative game can be hard to characterize.

The authors design each agent’s learning environment so that an optimal solution to the global objective coincides with a Nash equilibrium of the local agents. The society operates through economic transactions: agents buy and sell the right to act on the environment’s state. These transactions allow the agents to learn the credit-assignment process itself, linking local exchanges to responsibility for the collective outcome.

The framework yields a class of decentralized reinforcement learning algorithms applicable to standard reinforcement learning, option selection in semi-Markov decision processes, and dynamic construction of computation graphs. The authors also demonstrate potential transfer-learning benefits from the society’s modular structure. The equilibrium result establishes compatibility between global optimality and local incentives; it does not state that every possible equilibrium is globally optimal.
icml-2020-decentralized-reinforcement-le.tldr: An economic mechanism aligns specialized agents’ local incentives with a globally optimal reinforcement learning solution at a Nash equilibrium.

paragraphs: Deep Reasoning Networks address pattern de-mixing: recovering individual components from observations in which several patterns overlap. The framework combines neural learning with constraint reasoning, typically with no supervision or very weak supervision. Its main idea is to use known problem structure during learning, so the network’s interpretation of a mixture is guided by relationships that its components should satisfy.

The authors tightly integrate these constraints with stochastic-gradient optimization in an end-to-end system. They first introduce the approach through overlapping handwritten Sudoku puzzles, a simpler analogue of their scientific application. On this task, the reported digit accuracy is 100%, with nearly perfect recovery of the mixed puzzles, exceeding the supervised MNIST de-mixing models used for comparison.

The motivating application is inferring crystal structures from X-ray diffraction data. Here, the authors report substantial improvements over existing methods and expert capabilities, recovering structures that are more precise and physically meaningful. Together, the two applications illustrate how constraint reasoning can help separate ambiguous observations by bringing domain knowledge directly into neural optimization.
icml-2020-deep-reasoning-networks-for-un.tldr: Deep Reasoning Networks combine neural optimization with domain constraints to recover overlapping patterns in Sudoku puzzles and crystal-structure data.

paragraphs: Text classifiers commonly treat category labels as identifiers, leaving their meanings implicit. This paper makes the meaning of each category part of the classifier’s input. Every label receives a textual description, and the model evaluates a document together with that description to decide whether the label applies. Classification thus becomes a description-conditioned decision about the text.

Descriptions can come from hand-written templates or from abstractive and extractive models using reinforcement learning. The description and document are concatenated before being passed to the classifier. The authors argue that this encourages the model to focus on the portions of the document most relevant to the current label, interpreting the effect as a hard form of attention.

The reported experiments show significant gains over strong baselines across single-label classification, multi-label classification, and sentiment analysis involving multiple aspects. The contribution is therefore both a reformulation of the input and a strategy for supplying useful category descriptions. Its stated findings suggest that explicit information about what a label means can improve classification across several task formats.
icml-2020-description-based-text-classif.tldr: Pairing text with explicit category descriptions improves classification by directing the model toward information relevant to each label.

paragraphs: A document’s topics provide context that extends beyond individual sentences. This paper develops a language-understanding framework that uses this broader context while retaining information about which topics relate to each sentence. The motivation is that a document-level mixture of topics alone leaves out the topical discourse occurring within the document.

The proposed neural composite language model jointly learns topic and language models. It combines latent topic proportions with an explainable representation consisting of key terms associated with each topic. It also models sentence-topic relationships alongside document-topic relationships. This gives the language model access both to an overall account of the document’s subject matter and to topic information tied to particular sentences.

Experiments cover language modeling, word sense disambiguation, document classification, retrieval, and text generation. Across these tasks, the authors report evidence that the combined framework improves language understanding. The approach matters because it brings interpretable topic content and sentence-level topical context into the same learning system, extending the use of topic information beyond a single document-wide representation.
icml-2020-explainable-and-discourse-topi.tldr: A joint topic-and-language model combines topic keywords, document context, and sentence-level topic associations to improve language-understanding tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies how reinforcement learning agents can acquire skills without a task-specific reward. Information-theoretic approaches to skill discovery connect this problem to empowerment, but the authors identify a recurring weakness: the learned options cover the state space poorly. Their theoretical analysis and experiments show that existing algorithms can leave much of the available state space outside their discovered behaviors.

Explore, Discover and Learn, or EDL, addresses this problem by changing how the optimization is performed. It retains the same information-theoretic objective used in the empowerment literature. This distinction is central: the paper shows that changing the machinery used to pursue an objective can address a limitation without replacing the objective itself.

In an extensive evaluation on controlled environments, EDL overcomes the observed coverage problem and reduces how strongly learned skills depend on the initial state. It also lets users specify a prior over desired behaviors. These results support a more controllable form of unsupervised skill discovery, where the learned abilities cover states more broadly and can reflect preferences about which behaviors should emerge.
icml-2020-explore-discover-and-learn-uns.tldr: EDL changes the optimization of an existing information-theoretic skill objective to improve state coverage and control over learned behaviors.

paragraphs: Fully parallel hyperparameter search selects configurations that can be evaluated together. Space-filling methods aim to distribute those configurations effectively across the search space. This paper examines the benefits of such designs and proves that Latin Hypercube Sampling and Jittered Sampling improve over random search only by a constant factor. That result motivates changing the distribution from which configurations are drawn.

The authors propose two ways to reshape the search distribution. Recentering applies when the distribution of the optimum is known, while a Cauchy transformation addresses the case where it is unknown. The focus therefore shifts from how evenly samples cover a given distribution to how the distribution itself should allocate search effort. The authors provide theoretical and numerical support for significant gains over random search.

Validation includes artificial experiments, clustering, and Salmon mappings, followed by more expensive artificial intelligence tasks. Reported improvements extend to attend/infer/repeat, video next-frame segmentation forecasting, and progressive generative adversarial networks. These findings indicate that distribution reshaping can improve fully parallel search across the tested settings, beyond the constant-factor benefits established for the two analyzed space-filling designs.
icml-2020-fully-parallel-hyperparameter-.tldr: Reshaping the sampling distribution improves fully parallel hyperparameter search, with different methods for known and unknown distributions of the optimum.

paragraphs: Cross-domain alignment links entities from different kinds of data, such as image objects and sentence words. This paper argues that attention-based approaches often lack an explicit training signal for alignment and produce dense matrices that are difficult to interpret. Graph Optimal Transport supplies a direct alignment framework by treating the two entity sets as dynamically constructed graphs.

The method combines two kinds of matching. Wasserstein distance addresses correspondence between individual nodes, while Gromov-Wasserstein distance addresses correspondence between graph structures. These distances can be added to existing neural models as regularizers. The resulting transport plan supplies sparse, self-normalized alignments, making the inferred relationships easier to interpret than a dense set of attention weights.

The authors report consistent improvements over baselines in image-text retrieval, visual question answering, image captioning, machine translation, and text summarization. The common contribution across these applications is an explicit objective for aligning both entities and their relationships. This lets alignment influence training directly while also yielding a structured account of which elements are connected across domains.
icml-2020-graph-optimal-transport-for-cr.tldr: Graph Optimal Transport explicitly aligns entities and their relationships across domains, producing sparse alignments and improving several vision and language tasks.

paragraphs: Imputer generates sequences through iterative imputation, filling in output information over successive rounds. Its number of generation rounds is constant with respect to input and output token counts. This separates the number of sequential generation steps from sequence length, an important property for a model intended to produce an entire output sequence through a limited number of iterations.

Training accounts approximately for alternative alignments between the input and output, as well as alternative orders in which output content could be generated. The authors develop a tractable dynamic-programming algorithm for this purpose. Its objective is a lower bound on the log marginal likelihood, allowing training to incorporate these possibilities without claiming to compute the full marginal likelihood exactly.

In end-to-end speech recognition, Imputer outperforms earlier non-autoregressive models and is competitive with autoregressive models. On LibriSpeech test-other, the reported word error rate is 11.1, compared with 13.0 for CTC and 12.5 for seq2seq. The results show that the proposed generation and training scheme can combine a fixed number of generation rounds with strong recognition accuracy in the evaluated setting.
icml-2020-imputer-sequence-modelling-via.tldr: Imputer uses iterative imputation and dynamic-programming training to generate sequences in a constant number of rounds, with strong speech-recognition results.

paragraphs: Selective rationalization explains a prediction by identifying a small subset of its input features. A common approach chooses a rationale that allows accurate prediction when the model sees only that subset. This paper identifies a problem with that criterion: a highly predictive subset may rely on spurious correlations, so predictive success alone can select an unreliable explanation.

The proposed invariant rationalization criterion introduces a requirement across environments. The selected rationales must allow the same predictor to be optimal in each environment. The authors formulate this requirement through a game-theoretic approach. The key change is to evaluate rationales through the consistency of their predictive relationship across environments, rather than only their ability to support a prediction in one setting.

Theoretical and empirical results show that the proposed rationales can exclude spurious correlations and generalize better to different test scenarios. The resulting explanations also agree more closely with human judgments. These findings connect interpretability with transfer across environments: an explanation can be more useful when the predictive relationship it captures remains applicable as the setting changes.
icml-2020-invariant-rationalization-0e28.tldr: Requiring rationales to support the same optimal predictor across environments can reduce spurious correlations and improve generalization and human agreement.

paragraphs: Designing a building structure involves choosing components that satisfy regulations while keeping building mass low. Conventional optimization repeatedly evaluates candidate designs with simulation tools, making the process costly when the design space is large and simulations are slow. This paper develops a learned pipeline for proposing the cross-sections of columns and beams.

The authors represent building structures as graphs and train the design system together with a pretrained differentiable structural simulator. Differentiability allows the simulator to participate directly in the learning pipeline. This connects the proposed structural choices with their simulated performance during training, supporting an end-to-end approach to learning how to produce designs.

The reported designs perform comparably to those optimized by a genetic algorithm, while satisfying all constraints in the evaluation. This supports the feasibility of learning design proposals for the structural problem studied. The motivation also extends beyond the optimization process itself: reducing building mass can lower material costs and carbon footprint. The stated comparison establishes competitive design performance, rather than a proof that every generated design is a global optimum.
icml-2020-learning-to-simulate-and-desig.tldr: A graph-based design pipeline trained with a differentiable simulator proposes building components with performance comparable to genetic-algorithm designs.

paragraphs: Many neural architectures borrow their structure from iterative algorithms but use the same fixed number of layers for every input. Traditional algorithms can stop when further iterations are unnecessary. This paper brings a similar capability to deep models, motivated by the possibility that some inputs need less computation or that additional processing can amount to over-thinking.

The proposed steerable architecture learns a feed-forward prediction model together with a variational stopping policy. The policy sequentially decides how many layers to use for each input. Because jointly learning prediction and stopping is challenging, the authors develop a variational Bayes perspective and a training procedure divided into an oracle-model learning stage and an imitation stage.

Experiments show improved performance across sparse recovery, few-shot meta-learning, and computer vision tasks. The contribution is a way to make depth an input-dependent learned decision while training the underlying predictor alongside it. The results support adaptive stopping across the tested applications, with the stopping policy serving as part of the model’s decision process rather than a single fixed depth chosen for all cases.
icml-2020-learning-to-stop-while-learnin.tldr: A jointly learned predictor and stopping policy adapt network depth to each input and improve performance across several evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning to control a linear-quadratic system when some transition parameters are initially unknown. The central measure is regret, which captures the accumulated cost of learning relative to optimal control. Earlier efficient algorithms in this setting had regret growing with the square root of the number of decision steps.

The authors give efficient algorithms with much slower, polylogarithmic regret growth in two specific scenarios. In the first, only the state transition matrix A is unknown. In the second, only the state-action transition matrix B is unknown, and the optimal policy must satisfy a non-degeneracy condition. The improvement therefore depends on which part of the system is unknown and, in the second case, on a property of the optimal policy.

A lower bound makes the role of that condition concrete: when it is violated in the latter setting, square-root regret cannot be avoided. The paper thus provides both faster learning guarantees under stated conditions and a boundary to that improvement. It shows that the difficulty of adaptive control can change substantially with the structure of the remaining uncertainty.
icml-2020-logarithmic-regret-for-learnin.tldr: Efficient linear-quadratic control algorithms achieve polylogarithmic regret in two specified settings, while a lower bound shows when square-root regret remains unavoidable.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning across a collection of stochastic linear bandit tasks drawn from a task distribution. Its goal is to select a learning algorithm that performs well on average across those tasks. The central question is whether experience with earlier tasks can improve the exploration and learning required for another task from the same distribution.

The authors modify OFUL by adding regularization toward a bias vector, using squared Euclidean distance as the penalty. This vector provides a shared reference point for learning individual tasks. They first analyze how the biased algorithm affects regret, then propose two strategies for estimating the bias in a learning-to-learn setting. The shared information is therefore itself learned from the task collection.

Theory and experiments show a significant advantage over learning tasks independently when the number of tasks grows and the task distribution has low variance. These conditions matter: the stated benefit concerns collections with enough experience and relatively limited variation between tasks. The results support learning a common bias as a useful way to transfer information among related bandit problems.
icml-2020-meta-learning-with-stochastic-.tldr: Learning a shared regularization bias improves stochastic linear bandit learning when many tasks come from a low-variance task distribution.

paragraphs: Gaussian-process optimization uses uncertainty estimates to choose promising evaluations, but scaling it presents two distinct costs. Evaluations take time unless candidates can be tested in parallel, and selecting those candidates can itself require expensive computation. This paper introduces Batch Budgeted Kernel Bandits, or BBKB, to address both costs through batch selection and a sparse Gaussian-process approximation.

The central technical contribution is a guarantee for tracking posterior variances. It allows BBKB to select increasingly large batches while preserving a no-regret guarantee. The same bound also determines when costly updates to the sparse approximation can be postponed. This makes uncertainty tracking useful both for choosing more parallel evaluations and for reducing how often the internal model must be updated.

The authors establish near-linear overall running time and near-constant amortized cost per step, alongside the no-regret result. Their experiments confirm substantial speed improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The paper’s significance is the combination: batch evaluation reduces experimental delay, while adaptive approximation updates keep the computation needed to organize those evaluations from becoming the dominant bottleneck.
icml-2020-near-linear-time-gaussian-proc.tldr: BBKB combines adaptive batches and delayed sparse-model updates to deliver no-regret Gaussian-process optimization with near-linear running time.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often assumes that an environment’s transition dynamics and rewards remain fixed. When they change, adapting to observed conditions can leave a policy behind the conditions it will face next. This paper proposes Prognosticator, a policy-gradient method that searches for a policy by maximizing a forecast of its future performance.

To build that forecast, the method estimates how a candidate policy would have performed at different past times and fits a curve to those estimates. It does not explicitly model the underlying changes in rewards or dynamics. The resulting optimization assigns unequal weights to past data. The authors observe that reducing performance on some past episodes can help identify a policy with better forecasted future performance.

In three simulated problems motivated by real applications, Prognosticator is more robust to non-stationarity than two online adaptation methods. The findings support forecasting policy performance directly as an approach to changing environments. They also explain why treating every past episode as equally desirable to fit can conflict with the objective of choosing actions for future conditions.
icml-2020-optimizing-for-the-future-in-n.tldr: Prognosticator optimizes forecasted policy performance by reweighting historical data, improving robustness in three simulated changing environments.

paragraphs: Graph-based semi-supervised learning uses relationships between examples to learn from a limited set of labels. At very low label rates, conventional Laplacian learning can become degenerate, making its outputs less useful. This paper proposes Poisson learning to address that particular regime, changing how the labeled examples influence the rest of the graph.

Instead of fixing label values at training points, the method places sources and sinks on the graph and solves the resulting Poisson equation. This reformulates the mathematical role of supervision. The authors prove that the resulting outputs are more stable and informative than those of Laplacian learning, and describe the method as efficient and straightforward to implement.

Numerical experiments on MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR-10 show better results than other recent semi-supervised methods at low label rates. The authors also introduce Poisson MBO, a graph-cut enhancement that increases accuracy and can use prior knowledge about relative class sizes. Together, the basic method and its enhancement provide ways to preserve useful label information when supervision is exceptionally sparse.
icml-2020-poisson-learning-graph-based-s.tldr: Poisson learning uses graph sources and sinks to make semi-supervised predictions more stable and informative when very few labels are available.

paragraphs: Policy-based reinforcement learning has achieved substantial practical success, but its theoretical treatment of exploration is less developed than that of value-based methods. This paper asks how policy optimization can incorporate exploration while retaining an efficiency guarantee. It proposes OPPO, an optimistic variant of Proximal Policy Optimization, to connect policy improvement with a principled exploration mechanism.

OPPO follows an optimistic version of the policy-gradient direction. The authors analyze episodic Markov decision processes with linear function approximation, unknown transitions, and adversarial rewards under full-information feedback. These conditions define the setting of the result; in particular, the reward-feedback assumption is part of the guarantee rather than an incidental implementation detail.

The regret bound is Õ(√(d²H³T)), where d is feature dimension, H is episode length, and T is the total number of interaction steps. For fixed dimension and horizon, this bound grows sublinearly in interaction time. The authors identify OPPO, to their knowledge, as the first provably efficient policy-optimization algorithm that explores. The contribution is a theoretical exploration guarantee for policy optimization in the specified setting.
icml-2020-provably-efficient-exploration.tldr: OPPO adds optimism to policy optimization and proves a sublinear regret bound for exploration in a specified linear episodic reinforcement-learning setting.

paragraphs: Positive-unlabeled learning trains a binary classifier from a few known positive examples and many examples whose labels are unknown. This paper argues that existing risk-estimation methods overlook a useful source of supervision: the model’s own developing predictions. Self-PU combines positive-unlabeled learning with self-training so that the training process can make use of that information.

The framework has three components. A self-paced procedure progressively identifies confident positive and negative examples and augments training with them. An instance-aware loss adjusts the weighting of examples. A self-distillation scheme uses teacher-student learning as regularization. Together, these components address how to expand supervision, how to weight it, and how to regularize the resulting learning process.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on positive-unlabeled benchmarks based on MNIST and CIFAR10. They also evaluate the framework on brain-image classification for Alzheimer’s disease, reporting significant gains over existing methods on the ADNI database. These results support using the model’s own confidence and teacher-student training to improve learning when explicit negative labels are unavailable.
icml-2020-self-pu-self-boosted-and-calib.tldr: Self-PU improves positive-unlabeled classification through confident-example selection, instance-aware reweighting, and teacher-student regularization.

paragraphs: Traditional investment factors use reported company fundamentals such as revenue, earnings, and debt. This paper investigates using forecasts of those fundamentals instead. It begins with an oracle simulation showing that factors calculated from future fundamentals would produce much stronger portfolios. That experiment motivates forecasting, while keeping perfect knowledge of the future distinct from the predictions used by the proposed method.

The authors train deep networks to predict future fundamentals from a trailing five-year history and substitute these predictions into traditional factors. They then incorporate uncertainty estimates from heteroscedastic regression and a dropout-based heuristic. These estimates inform portfolio adjustments intended to avoid risk, making forecast uncertainty part of the investment procedure rather than relying on predicted values alone.

In retrospective portfolio simulation, the uncertainty-aware model improves both annualized return and Sharpe ratio. The reported simulated annualized return is 17.7%, compared with 14.0% for a standard factor model, while the Sharpe ratio is 0.84 versus 0.52. These findings describe backtested performance and support the proposed combination of fundamental forecasts and uncertainty-aware portfolio construction in that analysis.
icml-2020-uncertainty-aware-lookahead-fa.tldr: Forecasting company fundamentals and incorporating prediction uncertainty improves simulated returns and Sharpe ratio over a standard factor model.

paragraphs: A predictive model needs useful confidence estimates as well as accurate predictions. This paper focuses on Bayesian neural networks using Monte Carlo dropout, which can provide reliable approximate uncertainty estimates on familiar data but become overconfident when target inputs have a different feature distribution. The authors address this covariate-shift setting using unlabeled examples from the target population.

Their approximate Bayesian inference scheme uses posterior regularization. Unlabeled target data supply pseudo-labels for model confidence, which regularize the loss computed on labeled source data. This allows the target distribution to influence uncertainty learning even though its true outcome labels are unavailable. The method requires only minimal changes to the underlying model architecture.

The authors report significant improvements in the accuracy of uncertainty quantification on shifted datasets. They demonstrate the approach by transferring prostate-cancer prognostic models across globally diverse populations. The stated benefit concerns how well model confidence reflects uncertainty under a change in input distribution, showing that unlabeled target examples can contribute useful information to that calibration process.
icml-2020-unlabelled-data-improves-bayes.tldr: Using unlabeled target data to regularize Bayesian model confidence improves uncertainty estimates when target feature distributions differ from training data.
